column4: Those who spend their wealth by night and day, secretly and openly, bring together the two pairs that the section explicitly connects: night/day and hidden/open giving.
When God grants them bounty, they become stingy with it and turn away in aversion, joining the miser's refusal to give with the bodily and inward turn found in surah 92.
The ayah first identifies those who withhold when called to spend and then warns that if the community turns away God will replace it, gathering miserliness and tawallī in one address.
Moses sets himself toward Midian and asks his Lord to guide him to the even way; directed movement, the face-root, and hoped-for guidance form one travel scene.
The person who worships God on an edge is settled by benefit but, when tested, turns back on his face and loses both worlds; the face reveals an unstable direction governed by immediate satisfaction.
The ayah describes the worst wrong as denying God's signs and turning aside from them, explicitly coupling takdhīb with a refusal to face the guidance and mercy that have arrived.
When the one Lord is mentioned in the Quran, the hearers turn their backs and flee in aversion; coverings on hearts and heaviness in ears make the bodily retreat also a refusal to listen.
Most people turn away from the Quran's good news and warning so that they do not hear, an exact instance of the section's nonbodily turn through failed listening.
Each time Noah calls his people toward forgiveness, they put fingers in their ears, cover themselves, persist, and grow proud; refusal to hear is rendered as a sequence of bodily evasions.
On the Day of Resurrection the faces of those who lied about God are blackened, bringing the face and the act of lying together in their final visible consequence.
After guidance has become clear, one who opposes the Messenger and follows another path is left to what he has turned toward; guidance, chosen route, and the two-directional root meet in one warning.
The question whether believers would turn back on their heels if Muhammad died makes bodily reversal the image of abandoning a commitment after its guide is lost.
The warned day is one when people turn their backs fleeing, with no protector from God, and the ayah closes by contrasting divine misguidance with the absence of any guide.
Whoever turns away from God's remembrance receives a constricted life and is raised blind, making loss of attention in the present become loss of sight at the end.
Whenever a sign from their Lord comes, the people turn away from it; the next ayah identifies this repeated aversion as denial of the truth.
The people deny the truth when it reaches them, completing the turn-away scene of 6:4 and promising that news of what they mocked will reach them in return.
A man comes running from the farthest part of the city to urge his people to follow the messengers, supplying directed and urgent movement for the no-payment and guidance claim in 36:21.
When the people see a sign they turn away and dismiss it as continuing magic, so visual reception immediately becomes bodily and interpretive refusal.
Some covenant that if God gives from His bounty they will surely give charity and become righteous; 9:76 exposes their later stinginess and turn as a reversal of this promised direction.
Gloomy faces on that Day form the visual counterpart to the radiant faces looking toward their Lord in 75:22-23.
Those gloomy faces expect a back-breaking calamity, giving their gaze an opposite anticipated end from the Lordward gaze of 75:23.
The deniers are veiled from their Lord on that Day, a precise boundary and reversal of the section's search ending in encounter with the sought face.
People who turn back after guidance has become clear show a backward direction chosen after the route is already known.
Moses commands his people to enter the holy land and not turn back on their heels lest they return as losers, opposing forward obedience to ruinous reversal.

Other communities will not be pleased until the Prophet follows their way, while the ayah identifies God's guidance as the true guidance; the object whose pleasure is sought can redirect the follower.
People swear to please the believers, but God and His messenger have the stronger claim to be pleased, distinguishing human approval from the proper object of the search.
Even if believers are pleased with the excuse-makers, God is not pleased with the defiantly disobedient, sharply separating human satisfaction from divine approval.
A building founded on reverence and God's pleasure is set against one founded on a collapsing bank that falls into Hell, giving sought approval a stable direction and its opposite a literal fall.
Those who deny renewed creation are described as disbelieving in the meeting with their Lord, directly negating the encounter at which the section's search ends.
The broken promise and repeated lying of 9:75-76 leave hypocrisy in their hearts until the day they meet God, carrying the failed giving-and-turning scene to an inverted encounter.
A powerless dependent brings no good wherever his master directs him and is contrasted with one commanding justice on a straight path; directed movement is measured by the good it produces.
The answer to the denied meeting in 32:10 states that death will take them and then they will be returned to their Lord, restoring the destination they reject.
The running believer asks why he should not worship the One who originated him and to whom all will be returned, giving the movement of 36:20 and unpaid guidance of 36:21 their final destination.
The disbelievers turn away from the very warning addressed to them, another clear case of departure accomplished by refusing reception rather than by moving the body.
The world's growth and fading are set against severe punishment, forgiveness, and pleasure from God in the Hereafter, locating lasting satisfaction beyond what visibly flourishes and passes.
Noah says his repeated invitation only increases his people's flight, preparing the concrete gestures of blocked hearing and concealment in 71:7.
Whoever turns away from the remembrance of his Lord is led into mounting punishment, making the turn's destination explicit.
